question: At what parameter scale can an adversary reconstruct every training input, rather than merely fit its label, from a trained random-feature model, and does the resulting threshold and attack transfer empirically to trained neural networks?

key_findings.claim: The paper separates the interpolation threshold from an input-reconstruction threshold: random-feature regression fits labels around p greater than n, whereas its experiments recover the n inputs of dimension d only after p reaches order dn.
key_findings.evidence: Across synthetic sphere data, CIFAR-10, and the opening proof-of-concept, training loss reaches zero near p=n while the permutation-matched normalized input error drops near p=dn. This is a claimed empirical phase transition, not an information-theoretic necessity result.

key_findings.claim: Under restrictive random-feature assumptions and p growing faster than nd log-squared d, feature-span inclusion forces each candidate input to be close to some training input.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 1 assumes n=O(d), sub-Gaussian fixed-norm inputs, and a smooth nonlinear activation with specified Hermite coefficients. If every true feature vector belongs to the span of candidate feature rows, then every candidate row is o(sqrt(d)) from a true row with overwhelming probability. The proof uses kernel conditioning, Hermite separation, and uniform epsilon-net concentration; linear activations furnish a counterexample.

key_findings.claim: The paper proves that candidate duplicates cannot hide a missing example only for the special case n=2, so the advertised whole-dataset identification theorem is incomplete for general dataset size.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 2 rules out two candidate rows both approximating one of two training rows, via a Taylor expansion and concentration argument. Remark 2 explicitly says the duplicate configurations grow combinatorially for n at least 3 and only conjectures that the argument extends.

key_findings.claim: The practical attack optimizes candidate inputs so the trained parameter displacement lies in their feature span, a weaker condition than the feature-span hypothesis used by the theorems.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 11 minimizes the squared norm of the trained parameter vector after projection onto the orthogonal complement of the candidate feature span, with candidate rows constrained to a sphere. Because the learned parameter is only one linear combination of training features, zero attack loss does not logically imply that every training feature is spanned; Figure 2 supplies numerical rather than theoretical support for that bridge.

anchors.section: From the theory to a reconstruction algorithm, Equation 11 and Figure 2

key_findings.claim: The reconstruction phenomenon transfers empirically beyond frozen random features to trained two-layer networks, ResNets, different classification losses, and several appendix variants.
key_findings.evidence: For CIFAR-10 two-layer ReLU networks and residual networks, the reported error declines when last-layer parameter count passes roughly dn. Logistic-loss random features and cross-entropy two-layer networks show a similar transition. The appendix additionally reports ViT, weight-decay, pruning, and wrong-candidate-count experiments, but no transfer theorem is provided.

anchors.section: Classification losses, Figure 8, and additional ablations

key_findings.claim: Activation symmetry creates an observable sign ambiguity that prevents exact reconstruction even beyond the proposed width threshold.
key_findings.evidence: The theory requires nonzero higher-order Hermite coefficients of both parities to determine input sign. ReLU violates this condition, and the CIFAR experiment reconstructs negatives of some images; adding tanh to ReLU removes the ambiguity in a reported appendix experiment.

method.core_idea: Characterize dataset leakage through the geometry of the span of random nonlinear features, then invert a trained model by searching for inputs whose features explain the trained parameter displacement.
method.mechanism: For random features phi(x)=activation(Vx), the analysis first shows that sufficiently many random coordinates make the span generated by n training feature vectors identify their input-space generators, subject to distribution and Hermite-spectrum assumptions. A second theorem handles duplicate candidates only for n=2. Operationally, the attacker initializes n dummy inputs, repeatedly constructs their feature matrix, minimizes the orthogonal projection residual of the trained last-layer parameter vector or parameter displacement, renormalizes candidates to the input sphere, and matches reconstructions to training rows with the Hungarian algorithm for evaluation. The same projection objective is applied to penultimate features of trained finite networks.
assumptions: The attacker knows the architecture, computational graph, activation, trained weights, and for trained neural networks the last layer at initialization.
The number n of training examples is known for the main attack experiments, even though an appendix probes misspecification.
Training inputs are independent sub-Gaussian vectors of norm sqrt(d), with n=O(d), for the theory.
The activation is Lipschitz with Lipschitz derivative, has zero zeroth and second Hermite coefficients, nonzero first coefficient, and two nonzero higher-order coefficients of different parity.
The theoretical overparameterization is p growing faster than nd log-squared d, stronger than the visually summarized p approximately dn law.
Optimization can find a useful zero-loss candidate set despite a nonconvex objective and despite zero projection loss being weaker than the theorem's span-inclusion premise.
Input norm and representation are known well enough to impose the spherical constraint; natural images do not literally satisfy the stated data model.
Last-layer parameter count is the relevant width scalar for extrapolating the random-feature phenomenon to feature-learning networks.

techniques.role: Connects nonlinear feature-span equality to recovery of the input generators in a high-dimensional overparameterized regime.
Uses nonlinear Hermite components and parity to isolate alignment with a single training vector and resolve input sign.
Obtains concentration uniformly over candidate inputs, producing the nd log-squared d sufficient width condition.
Turns a trained parameter vector into an optimization signal for recovering dummy inputs.
Optimizes candidate examples while preserving the norm constraint assumed by the analysis.
Evaluates set reconstruction using Hungarian matching and, for ReLU, an additional sign symmetry.

evaluations.setting: Random-feature regression on n=100 CIFAR-10 frog/truck images with d=3072 and ReLU features
evaluations.metric: Training MSE and normalized permutation/sign-matched reconstruction error as p varies
evaluations.result: Training interpolation occurs near p=n, while reconstruction error drops around p=dn; at p=10dn the displayed reconstructions are visually close to all originals
evaluations.baseline: The p=n label-fitting threshold and unreconstructed candidates below the proposed p=dn threshold

evaluations.setting: Random-feature regression on synthetic inputs sampled uniformly from spheres across multiple n and d choices
evaluations.metric: Training loss and normalized set-reconstruction error over 10 seeds
evaluations.result: Distinct empirical transitions appear around p=n for fitting and p=dn for reconstruction

evaluations.setting: Two-layer fully connected ReLU networks and deep residual networks trained by full-batch gradient descent on small CIFAR-10 subsets
evaluations.metric: Reconstruction error versus trainable last-layer parameter count
evaluations.result: Reported reconstruction error begins declining after last-layer width reaches roughly dn, including visually close recovery of 100 CIFAR-10 examples at 4dn for the two-layer model
evaluations.baseline: Narrower last layers that still interpolate because total network parameter count exceeds n

evaluations.setting: Synthetic binary logistic regression in random features and ten-example CIFAR-10 cross-entropy training in a two-layer network
evaluations.metric: Reconstruction error, training loss, and feature-span orthogonal residual
evaluations.result: Both classification-loss settings display a reconstruction transition near dn in the reported plots

limitations: Author-stated: proving that every global optimum of the practical loss is a permutation of the dataset remains open.
Author-stated: efficient convergence of gradient methods on the nonconvex reconstruction objective remains open.
Author-stated: the behavior in the intermediate regime n much less than p much less than dn is unresolved.
The theorem's no-duplicate guarantee covers only n=2, while the headline concerns reconstruction of an arbitrary entire dataset.
The theoretical feature-span premise is stronger than the one-vector projection constraint exposed by trained parameters; the crucial implication is supported only empirically.
The sufficient scaling is p much greater than nd log-squared d, while the paper describes an empirical p approximately dn law and does not prove tight necessity.
The activation assumptions exclude the main ReLU experiments, where sign-flipped reconstructions are explicitly observed.
Natural images, trained representations, convolutions, transformers, logistic loss, pruning, and weight decay fall outside the random-feature theorem.
The attack assumes unusually rich white-box access, including initialization for trained neural networks, and largely small known training sets.
Visual similarity and training-set-aware matching do not establish an attack's precision when the true dataset is unavailable to identify successful candidates.
No defense study quantifies the effect of differential privacy, regularization designed for privacy, finite precision, access restrictions, or realistic augmentation pipelines.
The experiments use parameter scales as large as multiples of nd; practical time, memory, and attack compute are not compared systematically with competing attacks.
failure_modes: Multiple optimized dummy inputs converge to duplicates of one training example and omit another, the exact gap not ruled out for n greater than two.
A zero projection residual explains the observed trained parameter vector without spanning the individual training feature vectors.
Even or odd activation symmetries make x and minus x indistinguishable in feature-span geometry.
The optimizer reaches a non-data local or global minimum despite the model being wider than dn.
An incorrect estimate of training-set size yields overlapping reconstructions or extra duplicates, complicating candidate selection.
Feature learning changes the penultimate representation enough that last-layer width alone does not predict leakage.
Augmentation, stochastic optimization, weight averaging, quantization, or missing initialization breaks the parameter-displacement equation used by the attack.
The normalized matching score looks favorable only after using unavailable ground truth to select permutations and sign flips.
Heavy-tailed or unnormalized data violate concentration assumptions and may leak atypical examples below the aggregate threshold.
reusable_insights: Distinguish fitting labels from reconstructing inputs: their dimensional requirements and privacy consequences can differ by a factor of input dimension.
Treat a trained parameter update as an element of a data-dependent feature span and test what information that subspace identifies.
Audit the logical bridge between an attack's optimized surrogate and the premises of its identifiability theorem; a zero surrogate need not certify recovery.
Separate set coverage from nearest-example quality so duplicate candidates cannot masquerade as whole-dataset recovery.
Check invariances induced by activation parity or architecture before interpreting low reconstruction loss as exact input recovery.
Report attack success without oracle matching or ground-truth candidate selection if the intended claim is operational privacy leakage.
Use width-by-sample-by-dimension sweeps and prospective threshold predictions instead of inferring a scaling law from a single fixed dataset.
Test privacy leakage at fixed total parameters under different allocation across early and final layers to determine the correct capacity scalar.
open_questions: Can feature-span identifiability and no-duplicate recovery be proved for arbitrary n at p proportional to nd rather than nd log-squared d?
Does every global optimum of the practical one-vector projection loss recover the training set, or are there explicit non-data zero-loss constructions?
What optimization conditions make projected gradient descent find the data solution, and how does required compute scale with n, d, and p?
Is p approximately nd a necessary information-theoretic threshold under a specified finite-precision observation model?
Which examples, especially outliers, can be reconstructed in the intermediate n-to-nd regime even when the entire set cannot?
What replaces last-layer parameter count as the scaling variable under feature learning, parameter sharing, low rank, mixture routing, or compression?
How does the threshold change with realistic augmentations, minibatch noise, Adam, pretraining, fine-tuning, quantization, and weight averaging?
Can a blind selection score identify true reconstructions without access to the private training set?
Which defenses reduce reconstruction while preserving accuracy, and do they alter span information or merely frustrate optimization?
Does reconstruction risk follow a smooth curve or a sharp phase transition on larger datasets where p cannot practically exceed nd by large factors?

competitive_landscape.title: Reconstructing Training Data from Trained Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Haim et al. derive an implicit-bias/KKT reconstruction attack for binary homogeneous classifiers and empirically recover a significant subset. The present paper instead uses random-feature subspace geometry, targets the entire dataset, and proposes an nd width threshold, but requires a different parameter-access equation and does not prove its practical objective recovers all data.

competitive_landscape.title: Deconstructing Data Reconstruction: Multiclass, Weight Decay and General Losses
competitive_landscape.difference: Buzaglo et al. extend KKT-style reconstruction to multiclass and convolutional networks, regression-compatible losses, and weight decay, and empirically study width effects. The current work supplies a random-feature identifiability analysis and a concrete nd threshold for a projection attack, while extrapolating rather than proving the trained-network cases.

competitive_landscape.title: Understanding Reconstruction Attacks with the Neural Tangent Kernel and Dataset Distillation
competitive_landscape.difference: Loo et al. prove whole-training-set recovery in an infinite-width NTK setting and study which outliers are recoverable, also linking reconstruction to dataset distillation. The present paper's main advance over that asymptotic regime is a finite random-feature sufficient scaling tied to nd, but its no-duplicate theorem is only for n=2 and its finite-network transfer remains empirical.

competitive_landscape.title: Simulating Training Dynamics to Reconstruct Training Data from Deep Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: SimuDy differentiates through simulated nonlinear training dynamics and reports reconstructing most examples from a trained ResNet, directly addressing regimes where shallow or frozen-feature dynamics fail. The projection method here is structurally simpler and motivates a capacity law, but assumes initialization and feature-span leakage and does not compare attack quality or compute head-to-head with SimuDy.

competitive_landscape.title: Provable Privacy Attacks on Trained Shallow Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Smorodinsky et al. prove reconstruction of a set containing a constant fraction of true training points for univariate two-layer ReLU networks and membership inference in high dimensions. The present paper proves a different high-dimensional feature-span identification statement aimed at full-set recovery and proposes an nd width law, but neither result yet gives a general finite-network whole-dataset theorem.

competitive_landscape.title: Reconstructing Training Data From Real World Models Trained with Transfer Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Oz et al. adapt parameter-only reconstruction to high-resolution transfer-learning models using DINO/CLIP embedding inversion and introduce clustering to select candidates without consulting the true private set. The current paper offers a cleaner random-feature scaling hypothesis and full-set synthetic evidence, but its main image experiments are smaller and its evaluation relies on oracle matching.

novelty_assessment: Author claim: this is the first theoretical result connecting the feasibility of reconstructing a whole training dataset to model size, yielding a law in which random-feature models leak all n d-dimensional inputs once p exceeds roughly nd; the induced attack also works across several finite neural architectures. Prior parameter-only reconstruction attacks, NTK-limit recovery theory, and empirical width effects already establish much of the surrounding phenomenon. Reviewer inference: the defensible novelty is the finite-random-feature feature-span identifiability analysis and the explicit distinction between the n interpolation and nd reconstruction scales. The strongest whole-dataset and universality wording should be qualified because the no-duplicate theorem stops at n=2, the proved sufficient rate contains log-squared d, the optimized parameter-vector constraint is weaker than the theorem's span premise, and all feature-learning extensions are empirical.
reviewer_notes: Read all 49 extracted pages, including both theorem statements and proof sketches, the practical objective, main experiments, conclusions, appendices, and references. Page anchors identify substantive claims in the paper rather than bibliography-only mentions. Six direct competitors were checked against primary arXiv, OpenReview, or official conference records on 2026-08-23; comparisons distinguish prior KKT attacks, NTK theory, nonlinear-dynamics inversion, provable shallow-network attacks, and real-world transfer-learning reconstruction.
